title: Symmetric matrices and variance
lead: Symmetric matrices, those equal to their own transpose, and what it means for a matrix to have an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors; then variance, a measure of how spread out a set of data points is, taken along a direction, and the covariance matrix that records it.
summary_html:
This section explored both symmetric matrices and variance. In particular, we saw that

  • A matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there is an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors. In particular, we can write $A=QDQ^T$, where $D$ is a diagonal matrix of eigenvalues and $Q$ is an orthogonal matrix of eigenvectors.
  • The Spectral Theorem tells us that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric; that is, $A=A^T$.
  • The variance of a dataset can be computed using the covariance matrix $C=\frac1N~AA^T$, where $A$ is the matrix of demeaned data points. In particular, the variance of the demeaned data points projected onto the line defined by the unit vector ${\mathbf u}$ is $V_{{\mathbf u}} = {\mathbf u}\cdot C{\mathbf u}$.
  • Variance is additive so that if $W$ is a subspace with orthonormal basis ${\mathbf u}_1, {\mathbf u}_2,\ldots,{\mathbf u}_n$, then $$ V_W = V_{{\mathbf u}_1} + V_{{\mathbf u}_2} + \ldots + V_{{\mathbf u}_n}. $$

exercises.prompt:
This preview activity reminds us how a basis of eigenvectors can be used to relate a square matrix to a diagonal one.

  1. Suppose that $\kD=\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}$ and that $\kveceone = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecetwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$.

    1. Sketch the vectors $\kveceone$ and $\kD\kveceone$ on the left side of Figure 7.1.1.

    2. Sketch the vectors $\kvecetwo$ and $\kD\kvecetwo$ on the left side of Figure 7.1.1.

    3. Sketch the vectors $\kveceone+2\kvecetwo$ and $\kD(\kveceone+2\kvecetwo)$ on the left side.

    4. Give a geometric description of the matrix transformation defined by $\kD$.

  2. Now suppose we have vectors $\kvecvone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecvtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ and that $\kA$ is a $2\times2$ matrix such that

    $$ \kA\kvecvone = 3\kvecvone, \hspace{24pt} \kA\kvecvtwo = -\kvecvtwo. $$

    That is, $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvtwo$ are eigenvectors of $\kA$ with associated eigenvalues $3$ and $-1$.

    1. Sketch the vectors $\kvecvone$ and $\kA\kvecvone$ on the right side of Figure 7.1.1.

    2. Sketch the vectors $\kvecvtwo$ and $\kA\kvecvtwo$ on the right side of Figure 7.1.1.

    3. Sketch the vectors $\kvecvone+2\kvecvtwo$ and $\kA(\kvecvone+2\kvecvtwo)$ on the right side.

    4. Give a geometric description of the matrix transformation defined by $\kA$.

  3. In what ways are the matrix transformations defined by $\kD$ and $\kA$ related to one another?

answer.solution:
4. $\kD$ stretches vectors horizontally by a factor of 3 and reflects them in the horizontal axis.

    4. $\kA$ stretches vectors in the direction of $\kvecvone$ by a factor of 3 and reflects them in the line defined by $\kvecvone$.

  3. The effect of the two transformations are the same when viewed in the coordinate systems given by the appropriate set of vectors.

exercises.prompt:
Remember that the Sage command A.right_eigenmatrix() attempts to find a basis for ${\mathbb R}^m$ consisting of eigenvectors of $\kA$. In particular, the assignment D, P = A.right_eigenmatrix() provides a diagonal matrix $\kD$ constructed from the eigenvalues of $\kA$ with the columns of $\kP$ containing the associated eigenvectors.

  1. For each of the following matrices, determine whether there is a basis for ${\mathbb R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors of that matrix. When there is such a basis, form the matrices $\kP$ and $\kD$ and verify that the matrix equals $\kP\kD\kPinv$.

    1. $\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -4 \\ 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.

    2. $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.

    3. $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.

    4. $\begin{bmatrix} 9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$.

  2. For which of these examples is it possible to form an orthogonal basis for ${\mathbb R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors?

  3. For any such matrix $\kA$, find an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors and explain why $\kA=\kQ\kD\kQinv$ where $\kQ$ is an orthogonal matrix.

  4. Finally, explain why $\kA=\kQ\kD\kQT$ in this case.

  5. When $\kA=\kQ\kD\kQT$, what is the relationship between $\kA$ and $\kAT$?

answer.solution:
Answer.

    1. There is no such basis.

    2. There is no such basis.

    3. This matrix is diagonalizable with

      $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \hspace{24pt} \kP = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

    4. This matrix is also diagonalizable with

      $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \hspace{24pt} \kP = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \\ \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

  2. Only the last matrix.

  3. $\kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 2/\sqrt{5} & 1/\sqrt{5} \\ 1/\sqrt{5} & -2/\sqrt{5} \\ \end{bmatrix}$

  4. $\kQinv = \kQT$

  5. $\kA=\kAT$

Solution.

    1. The eigenvalues of this matrix are complex so there is no such basis.

    2. There is one eigenvalue $\klambda=2$ with multiplicity two. The associated eigenspace $\kEtwo$ is one-dimensional so there is not a basis of ${\mathbb R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors.

    3. This matrix is diagonalizable with

      $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \hspace{24pt} \kP = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

    4. This matrix is also diagonalizable with

      $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \hspace{24pt} \kP = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \\ \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

  2. Only the last matrix $\kA=\begin{bmatrix} 9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix}$.

  3. We form an orthonormal basis by scaling the eigenvectors to have length 1. This gives $\kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 2/\sqrt{5} & 1/\sqrt{5} \\ 1/\sqrt{5} & -2/\sqrt{5} \\ \end{bmatrix}$, which is orthogonal since the columns form an orthonormal basis of ${\mathbb R}^2$.

  4. Orthogonal matrices are invertible and have $\kQinv = \kQT$

  5. If $\kA=\kQ\kD\kQT$, we have $\kAT=(\kQ\kD\kQT)^T = (\kQT)^T\kDT\kQT = \kQ\kD\kQT = \kA$. This means that the matrix is symmetric.

exercises.prompt:
Each of the following matrices is symmetric so the Spectral Theorem tells us that each is orthogonally diagonalizable. The point of this activity is to find an orthogonal diagonalization for each matrix. To begin, find a basis for each eigenspace. Use this basis to find an orthogonal basis for each eigenspace and put these bases together to find an orthogonal basis for ${\mathbb R}^m$ consisting of eigenvectors. Use this basis to write an orthogonal diagonalization of the matrix.

  1. $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$.

  2. $\begin{bmatrix} 4 & -2 & 14 \\ -2 & 19 & -16 \\ 14 & -16 & 13 \end{bmatrix}$.

  3. $\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 4 & 2 \\ 4 & 5 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.

  4. Consider the matrix $\kA = \kBT\kB$ where $\kB = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}$. Explain how we know that $\kA$ is symmetric and then find an orthogonal diagonalization of $\kA$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \hspace{24pt} \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{5} & 2/\sqrt{5} \\ 2/\sqrt{5} & -1/\sqrt{5} \\ \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$
  2. $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 36 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -9 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \hspace{24pt} \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 1/3 & 2/3 & 2/3 \\ -2/3 & 2/3 & -1/3 \\ 2/3 & 1/3 & -2/3 \\ \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$
  3. $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \hspace{24pt} \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 2/3 & 1/\sqrt{5} & -4/\sqrt{45} \\ 2/3 & 0 & 5/\sqrt{45} \\ 1/3 & -2/\sqrt{5} & -2/\sqrt{45} \\ \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$
  4. $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \hspace{24pt} \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 2/\sqrt{14} & 2/\sqrt{6} & 1/\sqrt{21} \\ 1/\sqrt{14} & -1/\sqrt{6} & 4/\sqrt{21} \\ 3/\sqrt{14} & -1/\sqrt{6} & -2/\sqrt{21} \\ \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

Solution.

  1. We have eigenvectors $\kvecvone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecvtwo = \left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -1 \end{array}\right]$ with associated eigenvalues $\klambdaone = 4$ and $\klambdatwo=-1$. We form an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, $\kvecuone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{5} \\ 2/\sqrt{5} \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecutwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}2/\sqrt{5} \\ -1/\sqrt{5} \end{array}\right]$. This gives

    $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \hspace{24pt} \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{5} & 2/\sqrt{5} \\ 2/\sqrt{5} & -1/\sqrt{5} \\ \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

  2. We find

    $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 36 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -9 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \hspace{24pt} \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 1/3 & 2/3 & 2/3 \\ -2/3 & 2/3 & -1/3 \\ 2/3 & 1/3 & -2/3 \\ \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

  3. We have eigenvalues $\klambdaone=10$ with associated eigenvector $\kvecvone=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ and $\klambdatwo = 1$ with associated eigenvectors $\kvecvtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 0 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecvthree=\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 1 \\ -2 \end{array}\right]$. Notice that $\kvecvone$ is orthogonal to both $\kvecvtwo$ and $\kvecvthree$, but $\kvecvtwo$ and $\kvecvthree$ are not orthogonal to one another. We can, however, apply Gram-Schmidt to create an orthogonal basis of the eigenspace $\kEone$. We can then form an orthonormal basis so that

    $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \hspace{24pt} \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 2/3 & 1/\sqrt{5} & -4/\sqrt{45} \\ 2/3 & 0 & 5/\sqrt{45} \\ 1/3 & -2/\sqrt{5} & -2/\sqrt{45} \\ \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

  4. We have $\kAT = (\kBT\kB)^T = \kBT(\kBT)^T=\kBT\kB = \kA$ so $\kA$ must be symmetric. Then we find the orthogonal diagonalization

    $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \hspace{24pt} \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 2/\sqrt{14} & 2/\sqrt{6} & 1/\sqrt{21} \\ 1/\sqrt{14} & -1/\sqrt{6} & 4/\sqrt{21} \\ 3/\sqrt{14} & -1/\sqrt{6} & -2/\sqrt{21} \\ \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

exercises.prompt:
We'll begin with a set of three data points

$$ \kvecdone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right], \hspace{24pt} \kvecdtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 1 \end{array}\right], \hspace{24pt} \kvecdthree=\left[\begin{array}{r}3 \\ 4 \end{array}\right]. $$

  1. Find the centroid, or mean, $\kvecdbar = \frac1N\sum_j \kvecdj$. Then plot the data points and their centroid in Figure 7.1.12.

  2. Notice that the centroid lies in the center of the data so the spread of the data will be measured by how far away the points are from the centroid. To simplify our calculations, find the demeaned data points

    $$ \kvecdjtilde = \kvecdj - \kvecdbar $$

    and plot them in Figure 7.1.13.

  3. Now that the data has been demeaned, we will define the total variance as the average of the squares of the distances from the origin; that is, the total variance is

    $$ \kV = \frac 1N\sum_j~|\kvecdjtilde|^2. $$

    Find the total variance $\kV$ for our set of three points.

  4. Now plot the projections of the demeaned data onto the $x$ and $y$ axes using Figure 7.1.14 and find the variances $\kVx$ and $\kVy$ of the projected points.

  5. Which of the variances, $\kVx$ and $\kVy$, is larger and how does the plot of the projected points explain your response?

  6. What do you notice about the relationship between $\kV$, $\kVx$, and $\kVy$? How does the Pythagorean theorem explain this relationship?

  7. Plot the projections of the demeaned data points onto the lines defined by vectors $\kvecvone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ and $\kvecvtwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ using Figure 7.1.15 and find the variances $\kVvone$ and $\kVvtwo$ of these projected points.

  8. What is the relationship between the total variance $\kV$ and $\kVvone$ and $\kVvtwo$? How does the Pythagorean theorem explain your response?

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\overline{d} = \left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$.

  2. $$ \kvecdonetilde=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ -1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecdtwotilde=\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ -1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecdthreetilde=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]\text{.} $$

  3. $\kV=8/3$.

  4. $\kVx = 2/3$ and $\kVy=2$

  5. $\kV=\kVx+\kVy$

  6. $\kVvone = 7/3$

    $\kVvtwo = 1/3$

  7. $\kV = \kVvone + \kVvtwo$

Solution.

  1. The centroid is $\overline{d} = \left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$.

  2. The demeaned data points are

    $$ \kvecdonetilde=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ -1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecdtwotilde=\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ -1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecdthreetilde=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]\text{.} $$

  3. The total variance is $\kV=8/3$.

  4. We find $\kVx = 2/3$ and $\kVy=2$. Notice that $\kVy$ is larger because the points are more spread out in the vertical direction.

  5. We have $\kV=\kVx+\kVy$ due to the Pythagorean theorem.

  6. The points projected onto the line defined by $\kvecvone$ are $\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ -1 \end{array}\right]$, $\left[\begin{array}{r}-1/2 \\ -1/2 \end{array}\right]$, and $\left[\begin{array}{r}3/2 \\ 3/2 \end{array}\right]$. This gives the variance $\kVvone = 7/3$.

    The points projected onto the line defined by $\kvecvtwo$ are $\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ 0 \end{array}\right]$, $\left[\begin{array}{r}1/2 \\ -1/2 \end{array}\right]$, and $\left[\begin{array}{r}-1/2 \\ 1/2 \end{array}\right]$. This gives the variance $\kVvtwo = 1/3$.

  7. Once again, $\kV = \kVvone + \kVvtwo$ because of the Pythagorean theorem.

exercises.prompt:
Let's return to the dataset from the previous activity in which we have demeaned data points:

$$ \kvecdonetilde=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ -1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecdtwotilde=\left[\begin{array}{r}0 \\ -1 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecdthreetilde=\left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]. $$

Our goal is to compute the variance $\kVu$ in the direction defined by a unit vector $\kvecu$. To begin, form the demeaned data matrix

$$ \kA = \begin{bmatrix} \kvecdonetilde & \kvecdtwotilde & \kvecdthreetilde \end{bmatrix} $$

and suppose that $\kvecu$ is a unit vector.

  1. Write the vector $\kAT\kvecu$ in terms of the dot products $\kvecdjtilde\cdot\kvecu$.

  2. Explain why $\kVu = \frac13|\kAT\kvecu|^2$.

  3. Apply Proposition 7.1.10 to explain why

    $$ \kVu = \frac13|\kAT\kvecu|^2 = \frac13 (\kAT\kvecu)\cdot(\kAT\kvecu) = \kvecu^T\left(\frac13 \kA\kAT\right)\kvecu = \kvecu\cdot\left(\frac13 \kA\kAT\right)\kvecu $$

  4. In general, the matrix $\kC=\frac1N~\kA\kAT$ is called the covariance matrix of the dataset, and it is useful because the variance $\kVu = \kvecu\cdot(\kC\kvecu)$, as we have just seen. Find the matrix $\kC$ for our dataset with three points.

  5. Use the covariance matrix to find the variance $\kVuone$ when $\kvecuone=\left[\begin{array}{r}1/\sqrt{5} \\ 2/\sqrt{5} \end{array}\right]$.

  6. Use the covariance matrix to find the variance $\kVutwo$ when $\kvecutwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-2/\sqrt{5} \\ 1/\sqrt{5} \end{array}\right]$. Since $\kvecuone$ and $\kvecutwo$ are orthogonal, verify that the sum of $\kVuone$ and $\kVutwo$ gives the total variance.

  7. Explain why the covariance matrix $\kC$ is a symmetric matrix.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\kAT\kvecu=\left[\begin{array}{r}\kvecdonetilde\cdot\kvecu \\ \kvecdtwotilde\cdot\kvecu \\ \kvecdthreetilde\cdot\kvecu \end{array}\right]$

  2. $$ \kVu = \frac13\left((\kvecdonetilde\cdot\kvecu)^2 + (\kvecdtwotilde\cdot\kvecu)^2 + (\kvecdthreetilde\cdot\kvecu)^2\right) = \frac13|\kAT\kvecu|^2\text{.} $$
  3. $$ \frac13(\kAT\kvecu)\cdot(\kAT\kvecu) = \frac13\kvecu\cdot(\kAT)^T\kAT\kvecu = \kvecu\cdot\left(\frac13\kA\kAT\right)\kvecu $$

  4. $\kC=\begin{bmatrix} 2/3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$

  5. $\kVuone = 38/15$

  6. $\kVutwo = 2/15$.

  7. $\kCT = \left(\frac13 \kA\kAT\right)^T = \frac13(\kAT)^T\kAT = \frac13 \kA\kAT = \kC$

Solution.

  1. $\kAT\kvecu=\left[\begin{array}{r}\kvecdonetilde\cdot\kvecu \\ \kvecdtwotilde\cdot\kvecu \\ \kvecdthreetilde\cdot\kvecu \end{array}\right]$

  2. Projecting $\kvecdjtilde$ onto $\kvecu$ gives $(\kvecdjtilde\cdot\kvecu)\kvecu$, whose length squared is $(\kvecdjtilde\cdot\kvecu)^2$. Then

    $$ \kVu = \frac13\left((\kvecdonetilde\cdot\kvecu)^2 + (\kvecdtwotilde\cdot\kvecu)^2 + (\kvecdthreetilde\cdot\kvecu)^2\right) = \frac13|\kAT\kvecu|^2\text{.} $$
  3. $$ \frac13(\kAT\kvecu)\cdot(\kAT\kvecu) = \frac13\kvecu\cdot(\kAT)^T\kAT\kvecu = \kvecu\cdot\left(\frac13\kA\kAT\right)\kvecu $$

  4. $\kC=\begin{bmatrix} 2/3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$

  5. $\kVuone = 38/15$

  6. $\kVutwo = 2/15$. Then $\kVuone+\kVutwo = 8/3$, which is the total variance.

  7. $\kCT = \left(\frac13 \kA\kAT\right)^T = \frac13(\kAT)^T\kAT = \frac13 \kA\kAT = \kC$

exercises.prompt:
1. Evaluating the following Sage cell loads a dataset consisting of 100 demeaned data points and provides a plot of them. It also provides the demeaned data matrix $\kA$.

    import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/davidaustinm/ula_modules/master/data/variance-data.csv', header=None)
data = [vector(row) for row in df.values]
A = matrix(data).T
list_plot(data, size=20, color='blue', aspect_ratio=1)

    What is the shape of the covariance matrix $\kC$? Find $\kC$ and verify your response.

  2. By visually inspecting the data, determine which is larger, $\kVx$ or $\kVy$. Then compute both of these quantities to verify your response.

  3. What is the total variance $\kV$?

  4. In approximately what direction is the variance greatest? Choose a reasonable vector $\kvecu$ that points in approximately that direction and find $\kVu$.

  5. In approximately what direction is the variance smallest? Choose a reasonable vector $\kvecw$ that points in approximately that direction and find $\kVw$.

  6. How are the directions $\kvecu$ and $\kvecw$ in the last two parts of this problem related to one another? Why does this relationship hold?

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\kC=\begin{bmatrix} 1.38 & 0.70 \\ 0.70 & 0.37 \end{bmatrix}$

  2. $\kVx = 1.38$ and $\kVy=0.37$

  3. $\kV=1.75$

  4. If $\kvecuone=\left[\begin{array}{r}2/\sqrt{5} \\ 1/\sqrt{5} \end{array}\right]$, then $\kVuone = 1.74$.

  5. If $\kvecutwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1/\sqrt{5} \\ 2/\sqrt{5} \end{array}\right]$, then $\kVutwo = 0.01$.

  6. They are orthogonal to one another.

Solution.

  1. $\kC$ will be the $2\times2$ matrix $\kC=\begin{bmatrix} 1.38 & 0.70 \\ 0.70 & 0.37 \end{bmatrix}$

  2. $\kVx = 1.38$ and $\kVy=0.37$, which agrees with the fact that the data is more spread out in the horizontal than vertical direction.

  3. $\kV=\kVx+\kVy=1.75$

  4. It looks like the direction $\left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ 1 \end{array}\right]$ defined by the unit vector $\kvecuone=\left[\begin{array}{r}2/\sqrt{5} \\ 1/\sqrt{5} \end{array}\right]$. We find that $\kVuone = 1.74$, which is almost all of the total variance.

  5. It looks like the direction $\left[\begin{array}{r}-1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right]$ defined by the unit vector $\kvecutwo=\left[\begin{array}{r}-1/\sqrt{5} \\ 2/\sqrt{5} \end{array}\right]$. We find that $\kVutwo = 0.01$.

  6. They are orthogonal to one another. Since the total variance $\kV=\kVuone+\kVutwo$ when $\kvecuone$ and $\kvecutwo$ are orthogonal, $\kVuone$ will be as large as possible when $\kVutwo$ is as small as possible.

exercises.prompt:
For each of the following matrices, find the eigenvalues and a basis for each eigenspace. Determine whether the matrix is diagonalizable and, if so, find a diagonalization. Determine whether the matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable and, if so, find an orthogonal diagonalization.

  1. $\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 1 \\ -1 & 3 \\ \end{bmatrix}$

  2. $\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}$

  3. $\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 4 \\ \end{bmatrix}$

  4. $\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 5 & -4\\ 5 & -7 & 5 \\ -4 & 5 & 2 \\ \end{bmatrix}$

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. Not diagonalizable

  2. $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} & -1/\sqrt{2} \\ \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

  3. Diagonalizable, but not orthogonally diagonalizable.

    $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \\ \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kP = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 6 \\ 1 & -2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$
  4. $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -12 \\ \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{3} & 1/\sqrt{6} \\ 0 & 1/\sqrt{3} & -2/\sqrt{6} \\ -1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{3} & 1/\sqrt{6} \\ \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

Solution.

  1. This matrix is not diagonalizable because there is not a basis of ${\mathbb R}^2$ consisting of eigenvectors.

  2. This matrix is symmetric so it is orthogonally diagonalizable:

    $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \\ \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{2} \\ 1/\sqrt{2} & -1/\sqrt{2} \\ \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

  3. This matrix is diagonalizable but not orthogonally diagonalizable.

    $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \\ \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kP = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 6 & 6 \\ 1 & -2 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

  4. This matrix is symmetric so it's orthogonally diagonalizable.

    $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 6 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -12 \\ \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{3} & 1/\sqrt{6} \\ 0 & 1/\sqrt{3} & -2/\sqrt{6} \\ -1/\sqrt{2} & 1/\sqrt{3} & 1/\sqrt{6} \\ \end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that $\kA$ is an $m\times n$ matrix and that $\kB=\kAT\kA$.

  1. Explain why $\kB$ is orthogonally diagonalizable.

  2. Explain why $\kvecv\cdot(\kB\kvecv) = \left|\kA\kvecv\right|^2$.

  3. Suppose that $\kvecu$ is an eigenvector of $\kB$ with associated eigenvalue $\klambda$ and that $\kvecu$ has unit length. Explain why $\klambda = \left|\kA\kvecu\right|^2$.

  4. Explain why the eigenvalues of $\kB$ are nonnegative.

  5. If $\kC$ is the covariance matrix associated to a demeaned dataset, explain why the eigenvalues of $\kC$ are nonnegative.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\kB$ is symmetric

  2. $\kvecv\cdot(\kAT\kA\kvecv) = (\kA\kvecv)\cdot(\kA\kvecv)$

  3. $|\kA\kvecu|^2 = \klambda$

  4. $\klambda=|\kA\kvecu|^2 \geq 0$.

  5. $\kvecu\cdot(\kC\kvecu) = \frac1N(\kAT\kvecu)\cdot(\kAT\kvecu) = \frac1N |\kAT\kvecu|^2$.

Solution.

  1. Because $\kBT = (\kAT\kA)^T = \kAT\kA = \kB$, the matrix $\kB$ is symmetric and hence orthogonally diagonalizable.

  2. $\kvecv\cdot(\kB\kvecv) = \kvecv\cdot(\kAT\kA\kvecv) = (\kA\kvecv)\cdot(\kA\kvecv) = |\kA\kvecv|^2$.

  3. $|\kA\kvecu|^2 = \kvecu\cdot(\kB\kvecu) = \klambda\kvecu\cdot\kvecu = \klambda$

  4. Because $\klambda=|\kA\kvecu|^2 \geq 0$.

  5. In the same way, $\kC=\frac1N \kA\kAT$ so that $\kvecu\cdot(\kC\kvecu) = \frac1N(\kAT\kvecu)\cdot(\kAT\kvecu) = \frac1N |\kAT\kvecu|^2$. Therefore, $\klambda = \frac1N|\kAT\kvecu|^2$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  2. $\kC=\begin{bmatrix} 8/3 & 5/2 \\ 5/2 & 11/3 \end{bmatrix}$

  3. $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 5.72 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.62 \\ \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 0.63 & 0.77 \\ 0.77 & -0.63 \\ \end{bmatrix} $$

  2. $\kC=\begin{bmatrix} 8/3 & 5/2 \\ 5/2 & 11/3 \end{bmatrix}$ is orthonally diagonalizable because it is symmetric.

  3. $$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 5.72 & 0 \\ 0 & 0.62 \\ \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 0.63 & 0.77 \\ 0.77 & -0.63 \\ \end{bmatrix} $$

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that $\kC$ is the covariance matrix of a demeaned dataset.

  1. Suppose that $\kvecu$ is an eigenvector of $\kC$ with associated eigenvalue $\klambda$ and that $\kvecu$ has unit length. Explain why $\kVu = \klambda$.

  2. Suppose that the covariance matrix of a demeaned dataset can be written as $\kC=\kQ\kD\kQT$ where

    $$ \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} \kvecuone & \kvecutwo \end{bmatrix}, \hspace{24pt} \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix}. $$

    What is $\kVutwo$? What does this tell you about the demeaned data?

  3. Explain why the total variance of a dataset equals the sum of the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix.

Determine whether the following statements are true or false and explain your thinking.

  1. If $\kA$ is an invertible, orthogonally diagonalizable matrix, then so is $\kAinv$.

  2. If $\klambda=2+i$ is an eigenvalue of $\kA$, then $\kA$ cannot be orthogonally diagonalizable.

  3. If there is a basis for ${\mathbb R}^m$ consisting of eigenvectors of $\kA$, then $\kA$ is orthogonally diagonalizable.

  4. If $\kvecu$ and $\kvecv$ are eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix associated to eigenvalues -2 and 3, then $\kvecu\cdot\kvecv=0$.

  5. If $\kA$ is a square matrix, then $\kvecu\cdot(\kA\kvecv) = (\kA\kvecu)\cdot\kvecv$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. True.

  2. True.

  3. False.

  4. True.

  5. False.

Solution.

  1. True. If $\kA=\kQ\kD\kQT$ is invertible, then the eigenvalues are nonzero, which means that $\kD$ is invertible. Therefore, $\kAinv = (\kQT)^{-1}\kDinv\kQinv = \kQ\kDinv\kQT$, which says that $\kAinv$ is orthogonally diagonalizable.

  2. True. In this case, there cannot be a basis for ${\mathbb R}^m$ consisting of eigenvalues of $\kA$ so $\kA$ is not diagonalizable.

  3. False. This condition implies that $\kA$ is diagonalizable, but it may not be orthogonally diagonalizable.

  4. True. The eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix associated to different eigenvalues are orthogonal.

  5. False. This is only true if $\kA$ is symmetric.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that $\kA$ is a noninvertible, symmetric $3\times3$ matrix having eigenvectors

$$ \kvecvone = \left[\begin{array}{r}2 \\ -1 \\ 2 \end{array}\right],\hspace{24pt} \kvecvtwo = \left[\begin{array}{r}1 \\ 4 \\ 1 \end{array}\right] $$

and associated eigenvalues $\klambdaone = 20$ and $\klambdatwo = -4$. Find matrices $\kQ$ and $\kD$ such that $\kA = \kQ\kD\kQT$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

$$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 20 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 2/3 & 1/\sqrt{18} & -1/\sqrt{2} \\ -1/3 & 4/\sqrt{18} & 0 \\ 2/3 & 1/\sqrt{18} & 1/\sqrt{2} \\ \end{bmatrix} $$

Solution.

Since $\kA$ is not invertible, the third eigenvalue must be zero: $\klambdathree=0$. Also, an eigenvector associated to $\klambdathree$ must be orthogonal to both $\kvecvone$ and $\kvecvtwo$. We can find such a vector by finding $\text{Nul}(\kBT)$ where $\kB=\begin{bmatrix}\kvecvone&\kvecvtwo\end{bmatrix}$. This leads to

$$ \kD = \begin{bmatrix} 20 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix},\hspace{24pt} \kQ = \begin{bmatrix} 2/3 & 1/\sqrt{18} & -1/\sqrt{2} \\ -1/3 & 4/\sqrt{18} & 0 \\ 2/3 & 1/\sqrt{18} & 1/\sqrt{2} \\ \end{bmatrix} $$

exercises.prompt:
Suppose that $\kW$ is a plane in ${\mathbb R}^3$ and that $\kP$ is the $3\times3$ matrix that projects vectors orthogonally onto $\kW$.

  1. Explain why $\kP$ is orthogonally diagonalizable.

  2. What are the eigenvalues of $\kP$?

  3. Explain the relationship between the eigenvectors of $\kP$ and the plane $\kW$.

answer.solution:
Answer.

  1. $\kP$ is symmetric

  2. 0 or 1

  3. The eigenspaces $\kEone=\kW$ and $\kEzero=\kW^{\perp}$

Solution.

  1. If $\kQ$ is a $3\times2$ matrix whose columns are an orthonormal basis for $\kW$, then $\kP=\kQ\kQT$. This means that $\kP^T=(\kQT)^T\kQT = \kQ\kQT = \kP$ so $\kP$ is symmetric and hence orthogonally diagonalizable.

  2. If $\kvecv$ is in $\kW$, then $\kP\kvecv=\kvecv$ and if $\kvecv$ is in $\kW^\perp$, then $\kP\kvecv=0$. This means that the eigenvalues of $\kP$ are either 0 or 1.

  3. The eigenspaces $\kEone=\kW$ and $\kEzero=\kW^{\perp}$
